name: Diego Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy pipes, fittings and water heaters for Halvorsen Supply, a plumbing distributor out on the Route 9 industrial strip. I'm in at seven, check overnight stock levels on the screen, then call my main suppliers about late deliveries. After lunch I sit with the sales reps and work out what we'll order for the next six weeks. I've done it for 31 years and I know which supplier lies about lead times.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the phone calls, honestly. Old Mr. Brandt at the copper mill and I have swapped stories for twenty years. What wears me out is the new ordering software the owners bought, which flags my orders as errors, and the targets that rise every year while my pay doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype is what I'd have said two years ago, and I'd say it loud in the warehouse canteen. The software does the dull bits, like reorder emails, and that's about it. Prices and pay carry on, which for us means they carry on being too low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm still worried. My wife Marta works in a school canteen and we have maybe three weeks of money if one of us stopped. Hype or not, the owners already use the software as an excuse not to replace the girl who left in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I always have. I'd put in my hours, keep the supplier calls going and ask the union for a raise at the next round. I'd also try to put 100 a month aside, though I've said that for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mainly. Not scared of the machine, scared of the month when the car breaks and there's nothing in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money is the worry rather than the machine. What gets cut first in a bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the thing, with a thin cushion any bump is a crisis. Last winter the boiler went and we borrowed 1,800 from our daughter Inés, who's a nurse and earns less than she should. I hated asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you say is responsible for that squeeze?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd still be anxious, hype or no hype. I'm 58, the nearest other distributor is an hour away, and nobody hires a man my age to do the same job for the same money.

say: I'd tell colleagues AI is **mostly hype** and the software only does the dull reorder emails.
I'd say the real problem is **pay**, which hasn't moved while targets keep rising.
think: Money worries me more than machines: we have about **three weeks** saved if either of us stopped working.
The owners use the software as an excuse not to replace staff who leave.
do: Keep doing the supplier calls and ordering the way I always have.
Ask the union for a **raise** at the next round.
Try to put **100 a month** aside, even though I've failed before.
feel: **Tired** and quietly worried about one car repair wiping out our account.
S0.quote: I'm 58, the nearest other distributor is an hour away, and nobody hires a man my age to do the same job for the same money.
fieldNote: Thin **cushion** and few local jobs make him anxious even in the mildest world.
Blames the owners' targets and pay, not the technology.
Admits he borrowed money from his daughter and hated it, which shows how raw the money worry is.

steps.text: Keep calling the copper and fittings suppliers every morning at seven
Put 100 a month into a savings account
Cut the streaming and the Friday takeaway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a cost-cutting trick dressed up as progress. Companies say the software helps us, then they stop hiring. In the canteen I'd say we need rules about who gets replaced and when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job is exactly the kind they mean. Buying is checking prices, reading stock, and writing orders. A program can do that, and my boss knows it. I think I'm on a list somewhere, even if nobody's said so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union steward, Pavel, and ask what the contract says about redundancy. I'd also try to learn enough about the ordering screen not to be embarrassed, but I won't pretend I like it. And I'd stop buying anything we don't need, starting with the new tablet Marta wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a slow squeeze. Every quarter a little more of my work goes to the system, and I'm left to fix its mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a moment the software got something wrong. What did you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the software ordered 400 elbow joints we already had in the back. I caught it, but if I'm let go, who catches it? Nobody. Then it costs the company, and they blame the supplier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mention the union. What would you want from it in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the owners are most to blame. They bought a system to cut people, and the government lets them do it without paying a cent toward retraining. If it's strong change, then we need a union deal and public support, not a pat on the shoulder.

say: I'd say this is **cost-cutting** dressed up as progress, and companies need rules about replacing staff.
I'd push the union for a **redundancy** deal in writing.
think: Buying is checking, pricing and ordering, so my job is exactly what the software takes first.
I suspect I'm already on a **list** somewhere, though nobody has told me.
do: Ask the union steward Pavel what the contract says about **redundancy** pay.
Learn the basics of the ordering screen, reluctantly, so I'm not exposed.
Stop all non-essential spending, starting with the **new tablet** my wife wants.
feel: A **slow squeeze**, with more of my work going to the system and me left cleaning up its errors.
S1.quote: Last month the software ordered 400 elbow joints we already had in the back. I caught it, but if I'm let go, who catches it?
fieldNote: Expects the **team** to be cut and sees himself as one of those at risk, so alarmed despite sounding steady.
Blames owners and weak regulation; wants union and public support.
Concrete detail of the 400 elbow joints shows he values his own checking skill.

steps.text: Ask the steward Pavel for the redundancy terms in writing
Learn the new ordering screen well enough to spot its mistakes
Cancel the tablet purchase and trim the household budget
Write to the local representative about funding for retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, and then I'd say it's a disaster. Two years is nothing. Nobody in my company has a plan and nor does the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I lose my job inside a year, maybe two. A buyer's whole day is the thing the AI does best. I'm 58, so I'm too old to be retrained and too young to retire on what we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd go to the union and push for a joint demand: severance, retraining paid by the company and a pension bridge. Then I'd apply to the warehouse supervisor job, since the robots are three years behind. I'd sit down with Marta and add up exactly what we owe. We might sell the car and use the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry. Angry mostly. I've given this firm 31 years and I'd be a line on a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push for a joint demand. Who else at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marta that night that we're going to be fine, and then lie awake. My son Tomas is training as an electrician, and I'd tell him that's the best choice he made, because hands come last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Tomas about his own future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three extra years before robots would help a warehouse worker more than they'd help me. My work is the thinking part, which goes in 2028. But maybe the firm needs a few of us to supervise the machines for a while, and I'd fight for that.

say: I'd say **two years** is nothing and neither the company nor the government has a plan.
I'd demand **severance**, paid retraining and a pension bridge, together with the union.
think: I expect to lose my job within **a year or two**, because buying is the work AI does best.
I'm too old to retrain and too young to retire on our savings.
do: Push the union for a joint demand on **severance** and retraining.
Apply for the warehouse supervisor job, since robots come about **3 years** later.
Sit down with Marta, list every debt, and sell the second car.
feel: **Frightened and angry**, because 31 years of loyalty would count for nothing.
S2.quote: I've given this firm 31 years and I'd be a line on a spreadsheet.
fieldNote: Thinks his own job goes in **2028** and he has no cushion, so alarmed and sleepless.
Sees the robot delay as a real opening only for hands-on colleagues, and tries to move toward the warehouse.
Anger is aimed at employers and government, not at AI itself.

steps.text: Join the union's joint demand for severance and a pension bridge
Apply for the warehouse supervisor opening before it's advertised
Sell the second car and use the bus
Ask Inés and Tomas to share bills if my job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a bit slower, so I'd say we get to argue about it properly. Five years is enough time to make politicians do something if enough of us shout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be 63 when it lands. My job is gone by then, but I might scrape through on a reduced pension if I can hold on that long. I think it's the first one where I might make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the job as long as they let me and keep the union active. I'd cut our spending by about 200 a month and put it away, because I can't retire on nothing. I'd also help the younger buyers, Lena and Omar, learn the old skill of knowing a supplier, which a program won't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than two years, but still heavy. It feels like a clock behind everything I plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned arguing it out in public. What would you actually do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 I could claim a smaller pension. Marta would still be working part-time at the school. If we got the mortgage cleared, we could manage, but that's a big if.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years change about how you plan your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retraining at 60 to be what? A software checker? I'd rather push for early retirement with proper support. The warehouse might use me for three more years while robots catch up, and that would be enough.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** to make politicians act if enough of us push.
I'd tell younger buyers that knowing a **supplier** is a skill software lacks.
think: I'd be **63** when it lands, so I might just reach a reduced pension.
Retraining at 60 makes little sense; I'd rather fight for **early retirement** support.
do: Save **200 a month** by cutting takeaways and holidays.
Stay active in the union and go to every meeting about AI.
Teach colleagues Lena and Omar how to **read suppliers**.
feel: A **clock** ticking behind every plan, but a bit lighter than the two-year world.
S3.quote: I'd cut our spending by about 200 a month and put it away, because I can't retire on nothing.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a **path** to 63 and a smaller pension, so he moves from alarmed to anxious.
Wants political action and early-retirement support rather than retraining.
Still has thin savings, so every plan depends on the firm keeping him.

steps.text: Save 200 a month by dropping holidays and takeaways
Attend every union meeting and speak about AI job losses
Teach Lena and Omar how to judge a supplier
Lobby the local councillor for an early retirement bridge

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is nearly retirement. I'd say that's the version where it hits other people more than me, and I'd tell the young ones to take it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 by then and probably retired anyway. What worries me is what the world looks like for my kids, not for me. The money part of me is still scared, because thin savings don't grow by magic in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 65, then take whatever pension is on offer. I'd try to pay off the mortgage and put money into Tomas's tool kit. I'd also push the union to demand a fund for retraining, since a decade is long enough to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but only about myself. For my children it's heavier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be calmer about yourself. What stays a worry even then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inés is a nurse, so she's safe longer. Tomas is an electrician, which is hands-on and safe until robots catch up. I'd say to my kids: don't do what I did, and have six months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owners to start the retraining fund now, while they still have profits. If they wait until it's an emergency, they'll cut us loose and say there's no money.

say: I'd tell younger colleagues to take it seriously; ten years is **long enough** to plan.
I'd say owners should start a **retraining fund** while they still have profits.
think: At 68 I'd be retired anyway, so this one hits **my kids** harder than me.
Thin savings don't grow by magic, so the **money** fear stays.
do: Work until **65**, then take whatever pension is on offer.
Pay off the mortgage and buy **tools** for my son Tomas.
Push the union to demand a **retraining fund** now.
feel: **Calmer** for myself, heavier for my children.
S4.quote: I'd say to my kids: don't do what I did, and have six months saved.
fieldNote: **Retirement** falls inside the window, so his job looks safe, but family money stays on his mind.
Shifts from personal fear to advice for his children.
Still tied to the union and employers' responsibility.

steps.text: Work until 65 and claim the pension on offer
Pay down the mortgage with every spare 100
Buy tools for Tomas's electrician training
Ask the union to demand a company retraining fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years doesn't give a man my age any room, and my savings are thin. What would help is simple: a written severance deal, retraining paid by the company, and a pension that doesn't punish people who lose their job at 58. And I want the union in the room when they decide, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against technology. I'm against being treated like a cost. If they ask people like me how to bring it in, we'd do it better, because we know where the software goes wrong. Nobody asks.

headlineQuote: I'm not against technology. I'm against being treated like a cost.
portrait: **Diego Weber**, 58, buys plumbing supplies for a regional distributor and has done so for 31 years.
He is **progressive** and a union man, and blames owners and weak rules rather than the technology itself.
He **resists** new tools, never uses AI, and worries mainly about pay, a thin cushion and few jobs nearby.
His mood runs **anxious** to alarmed, easing only when retirement falls inside the window.
He lives with his wife Marta, and leans on his nurse daughter and electrician-trainee son.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because two years leaves no time for a 58-year-old with almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A written **severance** deal, company-paid retraining and a pension that doesn't punish job loss at 58.
The **union** involved in decisions before they are made.
